abstract: In differentially private (DP) machine learning, the privacy guarantees of DP mechanisms are often reported and compared on the basis of a single $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-pair. This practice overlooks that DP guarantees can vary substantially even between mechanisms sharing a given $(\varepsilon, \delta)$, and potentially introduces privacy vulnerabilities which can remain undetected. This motivates the need for robust, rigorous methods for comparing DP guarantees in such cases. Here, we introduce the $\Delta$-divergence between mechanisms which quantifies the worst-case excess privacy vulnerability of choosing one mechanism over another in terms of $(\varepsilon, \delta)$, $f$-DP and in terms of a newly presented Bayesian interpretation. Moreover, as a generalisation of the Blackwell theorem, it is endowed with strong decision-theoretic foundations. Through application examples, we show that our techniques can facilitate informed decision-making and reveal gaps in the current understanding of privacy risks, as current practices in DP-SGD often result in choosing mechanisms with high excess privacy vulnerabilities.

summary.idea: Introduce a divergence that measures the worst-case extra privacy vulnerability of one mechanism relative to another, with several privacy interpretations and decision-theoretic foundations.
summary.limitations: The abstract does not list the mechanisms or numerical vulnerabilities in those examples. The comparison quantifies a relative risk criterion rather than declaring all mechanisms with matching privacy parameters equivalent.
summary.problem: Two privacy mechanisms can share one reported epsilon–delta pair while having meaningfully different privacy behavior elsewhere, making single-point comparisons incomplete.
summary.results: Application examples reveal gaps hidden by standard comparisons and show that common DP-SGD choices can have high excess privacy vulnerability by this measure.
summary.tldr: A fuller comparison of privacy guarantees can reveal differences that a single epsilon–delta calibration point hides.

title: Beyond the Calibration Point: Mechanism Comparison in Differential Privacy

abstract: This paper studies the challenging black-box adversarial attack that aims to generate adversarial examples against a black-box model by only using output feedback of the model to input queries. Some previous methods improve the query efficiency by incorporating the gradient of a surrogate white-box model into query-based attacks due to the adversarial transferability. However, the localized gradient is not informative enough, making these methods still query-intensive. In this paper, we propose a Prior-guided Bayesian Optimization (P-BO) algorithm that leverages the surrogate model as a global function prior in black-box adversarial attacks. As the surrogate model contains rich prior information of the black-box one, P-BO models the attack objective with a Gaussian process whose mean function is initialized as the surrogate model’s loss. Our theoretical analysis on the regret bound indicates that the performance of P-BO may be affected by a bad prior. Therefore, we further propose an adaptive integration strategy to automatically adjust a coefficient on the function prior by minimizing the regret bound. Extensive experiments on image classifiers and large vision-language models demonstrate the superiority of the proposed algorithm in reducing queries and improving attack success rates compared with the state-of-the-art black-box attacks. Code is available at https://github.com/yibo-miao/PBO-Attack.

summary.idea: Use the surrogate's loss as a global function prior for Bayesian optimization, then adapt the prior's influence using a regret-based criterion.
summary.limitations: The analysis explicitly identifies poor priors as a possible problem. The abstract provides no query budgets or effect sizes, and the method assumes access to a useful surrogate model.
summary.problem: Black-box adversarial evaluation must find misleading inputs using only model outputs, and local gradient guidance from a surrogate can still require many queries.
summary.results: Experiments on image classifiers and large vision-language models report fewer queries and higher attack success than compared state-of-the-art black-box methods.
summary.tldr: An adaptively weighted surrogate-function prior improves query efficiency in black-box adversarial testing.

title: Efficient Black-box Adversarial Attacks via Bayesian Optimization Guided by a Function Prior

abstract: We discuss a model of consistent learning with an additional re(cid:173) striction on the probability distribution of training samples, the target concept and hypothesis class. We show that the model pro(cid:173) vides a significant improvement on the upper bounds of sample complexity, i.e. the minimal number of random training samples allowing a selection of the hypothesis with a predefined accuracy and confidence. Further, we show that the model has the poten(cid:173) tial for providing a finite sample complexity even in the case of infinite VC-dimension as well as for a sample complexity below VC-dimension. This is achieved by linking sample complexity to an "average" number of implement able dichotomies of a training sample rather than the maximal size of a shattered sample, i.e. VC-dimension.

summary.idea: Restrict the relationship among the data distribution, target, and hypothesis class, and relate sample complexity to an average count of possible labelings rather than the largest shattered set.
summary.limitations: These gains rely on the added restrictions and do not overturn distribution-free VC bounds. The abstract does not state the restrictions in enough detail to check a particular application.
summary.problem: Worst-case capacity measures can give pessimistic estimates of how many training examples a neural classifier needs to generalize.
summary.results: The resulting model improves upper bounds and can allow finite sample complexity despite infinite VC dimension, or require fewer samples than the VC dimension suggests.
summary.tldr: Distribution-sensitive counting can yield much tighter learning-sample bounds than worst-case VC dimension alone.

title: Generalisation in Feedforward Networks

abstract: A general analysis of the limiting distribution of neural network functions is performed, with emphasis on non-Gaussian limits. We show that with i.i.d. symmetric stable output weights, and more generally with weights distributed from the normal domain of attraction of a stable variable, that the neural functions converge in distribution to stable processes. Conditions are also investigated under which Gaussian limits do occur when the weights are independent but not identically distributed. Some particularly tractable classes of stable distributions are examined, and the possibility of learning with such processes.

summary.idea: Analyze symmetric stable and related output-weight distributions, and separately study when independent non-identically distributed weights still yield Gaussian limits.
summary.limitations: The abstract does not report finite-width approximation accuracy or practical training results; the main conclusions concern limiting distributions under particular assumptions on weights.
summary.problem: Infinite-width neural networks are often associated with Gaussian-process limits, but other weight distributions may produce different limiting random functions.
summary.results: The neural functions converge to stable processes under the stated weight conditions, and the paper examines tractable stable families and possibilities for learning with them.
summary.tldr: Infinite neural networks can converge to stable non-Gaussian processes, broadening the familiar Gaussian-process connection.

title: Beyond Gaussian Processes: On the Distributions of Infinite Networks

abstract: We introduce AutoJudge, a method that accelerates large language model (LLM) inference with task-specific lossy speculative decoding. Instead of matching the original model output distribution token-by-token, we identify the generated tokens that affect the downstream quality of the response, relaxing the distribution match guarantee so that the "unimportant" tokens can be generated faster. Our approach relies on a semi‑greedy search algorithm to test which of the mismatches between target and draft models should be corrected to preserve quality and which ones may be skipped. We then train a lightweight classifier based on existing LLM embeddings to predict, at inference time, which mismatching tokens can be safely accepted without compromising the final answer quality. We evaluate AutoJudge with multiple draft/target model pairs on mathematical reasoning and programming benchmarks, achieving significant speedups at the cost of a minor accuracy reduction. Notably, on GSM8K with the Llama 3.1 70B target model, our approach achieves up to ${\approx}2{\times}$ speedup \textit{over speculative decoding} at the cost of a ${\le} 1\%$ drop in accuracy. When applied to the LiveCodeBench benchmark, AutoJudge automatically detects programming-specific important tokens, accepting ${\ge}25$ tokens per speculation cycle at a$~ 2\%$ drop in Pass@1. Our approach requires no human annotation and is easy to integrate with modern LLM inference frameworks.
title: AutoJudge: Judge Decoding Without Manual Annotation
